title: The lute string
hook: Sona strains too hard; the Buddha asks how a lute sounds when its strings are too tight or too loose (AN 6.55)

segments.voice: Yesterday: maintaining, and your line, keep it going. Did yesterday's good get done once more, and did you enjoy it? Day three hundred eighty-eight.

On the walking path in a forest called the Cool Grove, a young monk has been pacing back and forth for so long that his feet are bleeding. The path behind him is stained. His name is Sona. He grew up wealthy and sheltered, and he has decided to make up for it by trying harder than anyone else. And right in the middle of all that effort, he's thinking about quitting. On day twenty you met the image at the heart of this story. Today, the whole story: the lute string.
screen: `THE COOL GROVE.` → `PACING UNTIL HIS FEET BLEED.` → `THINKING OF QUITTING.`

segments.voice: Sona's thought, the sutta says, runs like this. I'm one of the most energetic of the Buddha's disciples, and still my mind isn't free. My family has wealth. I could go home, enjoy it, and do good with it. The Buddha knows what he's thinking and comes to him. He doesn't scold, and he doesn't push. He asks about music. Sona, before you went forth, weren't you skilled at the lute? Yes, sir. When its strings were too tight, did it sound right? No, sir. When they were too loose? No, sir. And when they were neither too tight nor too loose, tuned to an even pitch? Then it sounded right, sir. In the same way, the Buddha says, effort that's too strong leads to restlessness, and effort that's too slack leads to laziness. So settle on an even pitch of effort, and tune the rest of your practice to it. The vīṇā, the Indian lute, isn't a random choice. Sona knows it with his hands. The Buddha teaches him in the language of his own skill. That matters for the four efforts we've just walked through. Effort isn't a dial that only turns up. Some days the string is slack, and you need to rouse yourself. Some days it's wound so tight it buzzes, and you need to ease off. The sutta says Sona took this to heart, practiced with balance, and before long became an arahant, fully awakened. The walking path stayed the same. The tuning changed.
screen: `TRYING HARDER THAN ANYONE.` · `TOO TIGHT, TOO LOOSE.` · `THE EVEN PITCH OF EFFORT.` · `EASE OFF, OR TURN IT UP.` · then, large: `TUNE THE STRING.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and check the string. Is your body tight right now, jaw set, shoulders up, trying to meditate correctly? Then ease it a quarter turn, and let the breath happen. Or is it slack, drifting, half asleep? Then tighten a little: sit up, and feel the breath more clearly. Keep tuning gently through the sit, a little looser, a little tighter, listening for the even note. The bell holds the time.
The lute string. The Buddha's lesson for Sona: effort too tight brings restlessness, too loose brings laziness. Tune it to an even pitch.
Your line: tune the string. Today, find one place you're straining and ease it, or one place you've gone slack and tighten it, just one turn. Day three hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Meditation teachers across Buddhist traditions tell Sona's story to students who push too hard or drift, and encourage them to adjust effort through a sit rather than force it.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. Sona, his feet bleeding from too much walking practice, is thinking of quitting. what do you do?
options: tell him to push through the pain.
ask him about tuning a lute.
send him home to his family.
fork.reveal: in AN 6.55 the Buddha asks whether a lute plays well too tight or too loose, and tells Sona to settle on an even pitch of effort.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit vīṇā: the Indian lute, whose strings the Buddha uses to teach balanced effort.

trapdoor: what you thought: the middle way means doing everything halfway.
what it means: effort tuned to an even pitch, eased or tightened as the moment needs.
what a scholar hears: in AN 6.55 the Buddha tells Sona to resolve on evenness of energy and to balance the faculties; the commentary says his feet were so delicate that hair grew on their soles.

sources.ref: Vinaya, Mahavagga V (the story of Sona Kolivisa)

notes: AN 6.55 paraphrased (Sona in the Sītavana near Rājagaha; bleeding feet; thought of returning to lay life; lute questions; evenness of energy; later arahantship). Confirm.
